summary:
Sri Lanka criminalises same-sex activity under Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and was applied to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the aggravated penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Formal prosecutions are rare. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 research found no convictions under the articles, and Outright International's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing: the US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions, and Outright International records harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services as frequent. In an August 2023 opinion for the International Commission of Jurists, Mathuri Thamilmaran identified the Sri Lanka Police as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, noting that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission had acknowledged this in preceding months, and arguing that administrative circulars cannot substitute for legal reform. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Section 365, and human-rights organisations have documented officers using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA people.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct. Outright International records these examinations as widely condemned as torture. No comprehensive anti-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. The national Ministry of Health issued a circular in 2016 to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the national human rights commission. A recognised identity card has been issued under that circular since June 2016. No surgical intervention is legally required, but obtaining the certification is described as bureaucratically onerous.

Prison placement for transgender detainees has no statutory rule. The national prisons department confirmed in October 2024 that current facilities cannot give transgender prisoners their own space, with separate accommodation planned only for prisons built in future. Placement is decided case by case: detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated according to their preferred gender where possible, while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender before placement, with the inmate's preference feeding the decision. Officials have stated concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing, and placement by birth sex remains the practical default in the current male and female ward system.

Gender-affirming care is difficult to obtain. Hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients. Patients report ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, raising treatment costs; hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught. The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as risky behaviour alongside drug use and multiple partners.

Family law recognises no same-sex marriage, no same-sex civil union and no equal rights for same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times. A March 2022 bill to ban conversion therapy was tabled by SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna and remained unsupported by the government as of July 2024, though professional college ethics apply; families are reportedly still regularly seeking doctors to administer such treatment to LGBTQ family members.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office's September 2024 Country Policy and Information Note on Sri Lanka assesses risk from state and non-state actors, state protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, and is the most recent detailed external country assessment of record. A joint stakeholder submission to Sri Lanka's third-cycle Universal Periodic Review, filed by EQUAL GROUND with Northwestern CIHR and GIHR, documents criminalisation and violations against LGBTIQ individuals.

Societal attitudes are more permissive than the statutory position suggests. Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, and politicians from both major parties have expressed support for LGBTQ rights. The Asgiriya Buddhist chapter has backed extension of rights and a constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa stated that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a head of state in the region. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation.

Public opinion on relationship recognition runs the other way. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed, and the country's Catholic leadership has rejected same-sex marriage, Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that such marriages are not a human right. A 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents identified as LGBTQI.

The August 2021 video of a homophobic counsellor prompted the College of Psychiatrists to clarify that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and to call for decriminalisation, noting that counsellors, unlike psychiatrists, are not regulated and require no degree.
localsOnly:
Community organisations with long operating histories include Companions on a Journey, founded 1994 as the country's first LGBTQ support group, the Women's Support Group founded 1999, and Equal Ground. These are the main points of contact for residents seeking support, documentation or referral.

Residents face the practical effect of Section 365 in dealings with the police regardless of whether charges are brought: moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings continues to cite the article, and complaints of sexual violence or blackmail may go unrecorded.

For a resident entering the prison system, accommodation follows the October 2024 departmental position: the recognised identity card issued under the 2016 circular is the strongest basis for placement by preferred gender, its absence triggers a medical assessment, and neither route guarantees a placement different from birth sex. Separate transgender housing exists only as a plan for future prison construction.

Transgender residents seeking medical care may encounter unfamiliarity or ridicule in public facilities, may need to use private providers, and are barred from blood donation if they are men who have sex with men. Conversion-therapy-style treatment remains available from unregulated practitioners despite the professional colleges' ethics positions, and the 2022 bill to ban it had no government backing as of July 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); its underlying content on criminalisation is assumed but not verified in this pass.

Several care-access, policing, public-opinion and family-law findings are carried from Wikipedia country coverage rather than primary documents, including the blood-donation rule, the 2023 opinion figures and the conversion-therapy bill status; these are unsourced at first hand here and would benefit from direct citation before publication.

The no-convictions finding dates from January 2012 and has not been reconfirmed by a later source in this inventory; whether prosecutions have been brought since then is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on entry or visa rules, border screening, or whether gender markers on passports or other travel documents are recognised for arriving visitors; visitor-facing document and entry treatment is not sourced here.
